title: How Autopsies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck mark the show's 400th episode by explaining how autopsies work. They cover why autopsies are requested (injury, delayed complications of injury, poisoning, infectious complications, foul play, or death with no attending physician), the difference between clinical and forensic autopsies, and the five legal manners of death. They compare forensic pathologists, medical examiners and elected coroners, citing a PBS Frontline article on America's patchwork death-investigation system and the history of the word coroner (from "crowner" under Richard the Lionheart). They walk step by step through the procedure: external examination in the bag, clothed and undressed, cleaning, Y-incision, organ removal, skull opening with a Stryker saw and claw hammer, and closing with a Hagedorn needle. They discuss estimating time of death (gastric contents, vitreous humor, rigor mortis, lividity, the time of death certainty principle), the cost and tools of autopsies, and problems in the system such as understaffing and lost bodies. The episode ends with South by Southwest and party announcements and a listener email about a health scare.

segments.title: Episode 400 opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts celebrate the show's 400th episode and tease the topic of autopsies, referencing a Fulton County medical examiner interview and the Faces of Death film.

segments.title: Reasons for autopsies and types
segments.summary: Autopsies are requested for injury, complications, poisoning, infection, foul play, or death without an attending physician. Clinical autopsies differ from forensic ones, which are the focus of the episode. The five manners of death are listed.

segments.title: Medical examiners, forensic pathologists and coroners
segments.summary: Forensic pathologists are doctors trained for autopsies, while medical examiners and coroners differ in qualifications. Coroners are often elected officials without medical training, and the chapter discusses the examples of Dr. Keisel's approach to determining cause of death.

segments.title: Problems in the death investigation system and origin of coroner
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the PBS Frontline article on the patchwork US system, including a New Orleans coroner controversy, underfunding, and the 1,600 counties. They trace the word coroner to the Old English 'crowner' under Richard the Lionheart.

segments.title: Autopsy procedure: external examination
segments.summary: The procedure begins with a new body bag and sheet, with the body moved by a morgue diener. Examiners note clothing, collect hair, fingernail and trace evidence, X-ray the body in the bag, and perform external examinations clothed, undressed, and cleaned.

segments.title: Internal examination and brain removal
segments.summary: The body is placed on a body block and the Y-incision is made. The rib cage is cut, organs are removed as one unit and weighed and sliced, and the stomach contents are examined. The scalp is peeled, the skull opened with a Stryker saw and claw hammer, and the brain removed.

segments.title: Closing the body, time and cause of death, tools and private autopsies
segments.summary: Organs are returned or incinerated, and the body is sewn closed with a Hagedorn needle. The autopsy takes about four hours. Estimating time of death uses stomach contents, rigor mortis, lividity, vitreous humor, and the time of death certainty principle. Tools and private autopsies are also mentioned.

segments.title: Announcements, listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts announce SXSW live podcast and a party, read a listener email from Austin about a health scare and listening to the show to sleep, and sign off with contact info.
